items.stem: Define the term "tied aid".
items.answer: Aid that must be spent on goods and services from the donor country
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: aid that must be spent on goods and services from the donor country. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why debt relief may not always lead to development.
items.answer: Savings may not be spent on poverty reduction; corruption or weak governance; countries may borrow again (new Chinese and Eurobond lending), leading to new debt crises, e.g. Zambia's default in 2020.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Savings may not be spent on poverty reduction; corruption or weak governance; countries may borrow again (new Chinese and Eurobond lending), leading to new debt crises, e.g. Zambia's default in 2020. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between multilateral aid and bilateral aid.
items.answer: Bilateral aid goes directly from one government to another and may be tied to donor interests; multilateral aid is channelled through international organisations such as the World Bank or UN.
items.markingKey: Bilateral aid goes directly from one government to another and may be tied to donor interests; multilateral aid is channelled through international organisations such as the World Bank or UN. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to debt relief for Ethiopia under the HIPC Initiative, explain how it illustrates debt relief.
items.answer: Ethiopia had about US$3.3 billion cancelled in 2004 and increased spending on primary education and health. Cancelling debt freed resources for poverty reduction.
items.markingKey: Context (Ethiopia had about US$3.3 billion cancelled in 2004 and increased spending on primary education and health.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Cancelling debt freed resources for poverty reduction. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to debt relief.

items.stem: Suggest two reasons why a TNC might choose to invest in Vietnam.
items.answer: Relatively low labour costs, a young workforce, political stability, free trade agreements (EVFTA, CPTPP), proximity to China and supply chains, e.g. Samsung's phone factories.
items.markingKey: Relatively low labour costs, a young workforce, political stability, free trade agreements (EVFTA, CPTPP), proximity to China and supply chains, e.g. Samsung's phone factories.

items.stem: Egypt received about US$20.6 billion in personal remittances in a year when its GDP was about US$389 billion. Calculate remittances as a percentage of GDP. Official development assistance (ODA) was US$2.4 billion: how many times larger were remittances? Explain one advantage of remittances over aid for households.
items.answer: 5.3% of GDP; 8.6 times ODA; remittances go directly to families (spent on food, schooling, housing) and are counter-cyclical.
items.markingKey: A1 5.3%; A1 8.6×; R1 R1 developed advantage.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that FDI brings more benefits than costs to host countries.
items.answer: Benefits outweigh costs where governments regulate FDI and link it to local firms.
items.markingKey: For: jobs, technology, exports and tax (Vietnam). Against: profit repatriation, low wages, environmental damage. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative"?
options: Government aid to promote the economic development and welfare of developing countries, given as grants or concessional loans
Moving business functions to another country, often to reduce costs
An IMF and World Bank programme from 1996 that cancelled debts of qualifying poor countries in return for poverty-reduction reforms
A company that operates in more than one country, with headquarters usually in its country of origin
items.answer: An IMF and World Bank programme from 1996 that cancelled debts of qualifying poor countries in return for poverty-reduction reforms
items.markingKey: C. "Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative" is an IMF and World Bank programme from 1996 that cancelled debts of qualifying poor countries in return for poverty-reduction reforms.

items.stem: Explain why FDI is concentrated in a small number of countries.
items.answer: TNCs seek large markets, skilled or cheap labour, good infrastructure, political stability and favourable tax policies, so FDI flows mainly to high-income countries and major emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: TNCs seek large markets, skilled or cheap labour, good infrastructure, political stability and favourable tax policies, so FDI flows mainly to high-income countries and major emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Remittances only benefit the families who receive them." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They also have multiplier effects in local economies through spending on construction, services and businesses, and they provide foreign exchange.
items.markingKey: They also have multiplier effects in local economies through spending on construction, services and businesses, and they provide foreign exchange. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a recent year the USA provided about US$63.2 billion of official development assistance; its GNI was about US$27,700 billion. Calculate ODA as a percentage of GNI and compare it with the UN target of 0.7%.
items.answer: 0.23% of GNI - below the 0.7% target

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A system of supplying components exactly when needed, minimising stock but increasing vulnerability to disruption"?
items.answer: just-in-time production

items.stem: Briefly explain why countries that export primary commodities often gain little from global trade.
items.answer: Commodity prices are volatile and often fall relative to manufactured goods; most value is added in processing and branding abroad; tariff escalation discourages processing in exporting countries.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Commodity prices are volatile and often fall relative to manufactured goods; most value is added in processing and branding abroad; tariff escalation discourages processing in exporting countries. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between downstream activities and upstream activities.
items.answer: Upstream activities are early in the value chain, such as raw material extraction and components; downstream activities are closer to the consumer, such as distribution, marketing and retail.
items.markingKey: Upstream activities are early in the value chain, such as raw material extraction and components; downstream activities are closer to the consumer, such as distribution, marketing and retail. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The following years of schooling completed by adults surveyed in a suburb of Quito were recorded: 8, 5, 16, 14, 5, 15, 5, 10, 2. Calculate the mean, median and range.
items.answer: mean 8.9; median 8; range 14
items.markingKey: A1 mean 8.9; A1 median 8 (data ordered); A1 range 14.

items.stem: A firm moves 40 tonnes of goods from Shanghai to Rotterdam (about 19,500 km). Emission factors: container ship 12 g CO₂ per tonne-km; heavy goods vehicle 80 g CO₂ per tonne-km. Calculate the emissions (tonnes CO₂) for each mode and how many times higher the larger figure is.
items.answer: container ship: 9.36 t; heavy goods vehicle: 62.40 t; ratio 6.7
items.markingKey: M1 tonnes × km × factor ÷ 10⁶; A1 9.36; A1 62.40; A1 ratio 6.7.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Global supply chains mainly benefit high-income countries."
items.answer: High-income countries capture most value, but supply chains have been a route to development for some emerging economies.
items.markingKey: For: value captured by design, branding and finance. Against: East Asian economies grew rapidly by joining supply chains. items.stem: Define the term "commodity".
items.answer: A raw material or primary product traded globally, such as oil, copper, coffee or cocoa

items.stem: Isabel writes: "TNCs only move to countries to exploit cheap labour." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Market access, skills, infrastructure and tax policies are often more important, which is why most FDI goes to high-income countries.
items.markingKey: Market access, skills, infrastructure and tax policies are often more important, which is why most FDI goes to high-income countries. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Global trade benefits all countries equally." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Gains are uneven; countries exporting processed and high-tech goods gain more than raw commodity exporters.
items.markingKey: Gains are uneven; countries exporting processed and high-tech goods gain more than raw commodity exporters. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe cocoa in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana and explain what it reveals about commodity dependence in trade.
items.answer: They grow about 60% of the world's cocoa, but farmers earn only about 6-7% of the value of a chocolate bar. Value is added mainly by processors and retailers in high-income countries.

items.stem: Suggest why cocoa farmers in Ghana receive a small share of the value of a chocolate bar.
items.answer: Most value is added by processing, branding and retail in Europe and North America; farmers sell raw beans at volatile world prices and lack bargaining power.
items.markingKey: Most value is added by processing, branding and retail in Europe and North America; farmers sell raw beans at volatile world prices and lack bargaining power.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that TNCs bring more benefits than costs to the countries where they operate.
items.answer: TNCs can bring large benefits, but outcomes depend on host regulation and bargaining power.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: jobs and skills (Foxconn, Samsung); exports and tax revenue. Against / limitations: low wages, poor conditions (Rana Plaza); profit repatriation and tax avoidance. A supported conclusion might be: TNCs can bring large benefits, but outcomes depend on host regulation and bargaining power. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Government aid to promote the economic development and welfare of developing countries, given as grants or concessional loans"?
items.answer: official development assistance (ODA)
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of official development assistance (ODA).

items.stem: Which country makes most of Apple's iPhones?
items.answer: China
items.markingKey: D. Foxconn and other contractors assemble most iPhones in China, though India's share is rising.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "labour migration".
items.answer: The movement of people across borders to find work, often temporary or circular
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the movement of people across borders to find work, often temporary or circular. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Debt relief has solved the debt problems of poor countries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: HIPC cancelled about US$100 billion, but by 2024 more than half of low-income countries were at high risk of or in debt distress.
items.markingKey: HIPC cancelled about US$100 billion, but by 2024 more than half of low-income countries were at high risk of or in debt distress. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Maya writes: "An iPhone labelled "Made in China" is mostly Chinese value." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Components come from many countries (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, USA) and design and profits are mainly American; assembly in China captures only a small share of value.
items.markingKey: Components come from many countries (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, USA) and design and profits are mainly American; assembly in China captures only a small share of value. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how migration controls can affect migrants' rights.
items.answer: Sponsorship systems such as kafala can tie workers to employers, leading to passport confiscation and exploitation; irregular migrants have little legal protection; temporary visas limit family reunion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sponsorship systems such as kafala can tie workers to employers, leading to passport confiscation and exploitation; irregular migrants have little legal protection; temporary visas limit family reunion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between FDI and ODA.
items.answer: ODA is government aid for development, often grants or concessional loans; FDI is private investment by companies seeking profit in productive assets abroad.
items.markingKey: ODA is government aid for development, often grants or concessional loans; FDI is private investment by companies seeking profit in productive assets abroad. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between offshoring and outsourcing.
items.answer: Offshoring is relocating activities to another country (whether owned by the firm or not); outsourcing is contracting activities to another firm (which may be at home or abroad).
items.markingKey: Offshoring is relocating activities to another country (whether owned by the firm or not); outsourcing is contracting activities to another firm (which may be at home or abroad). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Zara writes: "Labour migrants take jobs from local workers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many fill shortages in jobs locals do not want or lack skills for, such as construction in the Gulf or care work in Europe.
items.markingKey: Many fill shortages in jobs locals do not want or lack skills for, such as construction in the Gulf or care work in Europe. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Samsung's investment in Vietnam, explain how it illustrates FDI by transnational corporations.
items.answer: Samsung has invested over US$20 billion in factories near Hanoi, which make around half of its smartphones. FDI brings jobs and exports but profits flow back to the parent company.
items.markingKey: Context (Samsung has invested over US$20 billion in factories near Hanoi, which make around half of its smartphones.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: FDI brings jobs and exports but profits flow back to the parent company. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to FDI by transnational corporations.

items.stem: Using a named TNC, explain its global supply chain.
items.answer: e.g. Apple: designed in California; components from Japan (sensors), Korea (displays from Samsung), Taiwan (chips from TSMC), USA; assembly by Foxconn in China and increasingly India; global sales through Apple stores and online; profits largely retained by Apple.
items.markingKey: e.g. Apple: designed in California; components from Japan (sensors), Korea (displays from Samsung), Taiwan (chips from TSMC), USA; assembly by Foxconn in China and increasingly India; global sales through Apple stores and online; profits largely retained by Apple.

items.stem: India received about US$112.9 billion in personal remittances in a year when its GDP was about US$3,408 billion. Calculate remittances as a percentage of GDP. Official development assistance (ODA) was US$3.0 billion: how many times larger were remittances? Explain one advantage of remittances over aid for households.
items.answer: 3.3% of GDP; 37.4 times ODA; remittances go directly to families (spent on food, schooling, housing) and are counter-cyclical.
items.markingKey: A1 3.3%; A1 37.4×; R1 R1 developed advantage.

items.stem: Illustrative data for Sri Lanka: GDP US$276 billion; external debt US$184.3 billion; exports of goods and services US$87.1 billion; annual external debt service US$8.66 billion. Calculate the external debt-to-GDP ratio and the debt-service-to-exports ratio.
items.answer: debt/GDP = 66.8%; debt service/exports = 9.9%

items.stem: Between 1990 and 2000 the number of international tourist arrivals in a North African country changed from 6.2 to 7.4 million. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (7.4 − 6.2) ÷ 6.2 × 100; A1 +19.4% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: A data table shows the population of a county in rural Ireland: 2000 - 53,578 people; 2012 - 73,504 people. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (73,504 − 53,578) ÷ 53,578 × 100; A1 +37.2% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Tajikistan received about US$5.3 billion in personal remittances in a year when its GDP was about US$11 billion. Calculate remittances as a percentage of GDP. Official development assistance (ODA) was US$0.4 billion: how many times larger were remittances? Explain one advantage of remittances over aid for households.
items.answer: 48.0% of GDP; 14.4 times ODA; remittances go directly to families (spent on food, schooling, housing) and are counter-cyclical.
items.markingKey: A1 48.0%; A1 14.4×; R1 R1 developed advantage.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that Global supply chains mainly benefit high-income countries.
items.answer: High-income countries capture most value, but supply chains have been a route to development for some emerging economies.
items.markingKey: For: value captured by design, branding and finance. Against: East Asian economies grew rapidly by joining supply chains. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Examine the reasons why labour migration brings more benefits to source countries than costs in some places but not in others.
items.answer: remittances (Nepal, Philippines); skills of returnees
items.markingKey: Paper 3 (a) indicative content: remittances (Nepal, Philippines); skills of returnees; brain drain of doctors and nurses; family separation and dependency. items.stem: Examine the reasons why FDI brings more benefits than costs to host countries in some places but not in others.
items.answer: jobs, technology, exports and tax (Vietnam); multiplier effects
items.markingKey: Paper 3 (a) indicative content: jobs, technology, exports and tax (Vietnam); multiplier effects; profit repatriation, low wages, environmental damage; footloose investment can leave. items.stem: "Global supply chains mainly benefit high-income countries." To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the perspectives of different places and scales.
items.answer: High-income countries capture most value, but supply chains have been a route to development for some emerging economies.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 (b) indicative content - for: value captured by design, branding and finance; commodity exporters gain little.
